extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers, journalists, researchers, and activists interested in digital rights and the Electronic Frontier Foundation
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of the Electronic Frontier Foundation's activities, policy positions, awards, and guidelines it helped produce (e.g., content-moderation principles and evaluation scorecards). The page summarizes EFF standards, initiatives, and programmatic criteria rather than giving a single formal rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Santa Clara Principles (content moderation guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Santa Clara Principles: 'Statistics on removed posts should be publicly available. Banned users or users who have had posts deleted should be notified with clear reasons. Such users should have the opportunity to appeal and have that appeal read by a human.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EFF joined other organizations in writing these principles (on transparency and accountability in content moderation). The page also notes a later update/request including asking platforms (e.g., Facebook) to warn users who have interacted with sock-puppet law enforcement accounts. These principles emphasize public statistics, clear notice, and human-read appeals as evaluative standards for platform moderation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure Messaging Scorecard criteria (version 1.0)
rubrics_metrics.description: EFF released a Secure Messaging Scorecard which 'evaluated apps and tools based on a set of seven specific criteria ranging from whether messages were encrypted in transit to whether or not the code had been recently audited.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page does not list all seven items, but gives examples (encryption in transit; whether code had been recently audited). The Scorecard functioned as an evaluative rubric for messaging apps' security/privacy properties (version 1.0 referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: EFF Pioneer Awards selection criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The EFF Awards (until 2022 called the EFF Pioneer Awards) are awarded annually to recognize individuals who in its opinion are 'leaders who are extending freedom and innovation on the electronic frontier.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative standard for selecting award recipients — nominees are judged by contribution to freedom and innovation online. The phrasing indicates the award's core desideratum (extending freedom and innovation).

rubrics_metrics.name: EFF Cooperative Computing Awards thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The EFF Cooperative Computing Awards are a series of four awards meant 'to encourage ordinary Internet users to contribute to solving huge scientific problems', awarded to the first individual or group who discovers a prime number with a significant record number of decimal digits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The awards and thresholds listed on the page: $50,000 to first who finds a prime with at least 1,000,000 decimal digits (awarded April 6, 2000); $100,000 to first with at least 10,000,000 digits (awarded Oct 14, 2009); $150,000 to first with at least 100,000,000 digits; $250,000 to first with at least 1,000,000,000 digits. These are explicit, objective eligibility criteria for each prize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Busting Project process (two-phase challenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Busting Project 'involves two phases: documenting the damage caused by these patents, and submitting challenges to the United States Patent and Trademark Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initiative's evaluative/process criteria: identify and document harm caused by allegedly illegitimate patents, then file formal challenges at the USPTO. Launched April 19, 2004. The project targets patents the EFF believes 'suppress innovation or limit online expression.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy for paper audit trails for voting machines
rubrics_metrics.description: The EFF 'has long been an advocate of paper audit trails for voting machines and testified in support of them after the 2004 United States presidential election.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This states a policy standard EFF endorses for election technology (paper audit trails as a requirement for verifiability and security). It functions as a criterion for assessing voting-machine integrity and procurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to SLAPPs and advocacy for anti-SLAPP legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: EFF 'has long taken a stance against strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPP) as attempts to stymie free speech and advocated for effective anti-SLAPP legislation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses a normative/legal standard: SLAPP suits are illegitimate restraints on speech and should be checked through anti-SLAPP legal frameworks. It serves as an advocacy criterion for assessing litigation that chills public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation and defeat of 'abusive patents'
rubrics_metrics.description: EFF 'solicits a list of what it considers are abusive patents with intentions to defeat those that it considers are without merit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational/policy criterion: patents that the EFF judges abusive (i.e., lacking merit, suppressing innovation or expression) are to be documented and challenged. This states how the organization evaluates which patents to target.
